newsitem.title: TURKEY: Islamists celebrate Ottoman conquest of Istanbul.
newsitem.headline: Islamists celebrate Ottoman conquest of Istanbul.

text.p: Turks on Thursday mark the 544th anniversary of the Ottoman conquest of Istanbul in what is expected to become a show of strengh by the battered government's Islamist wing.

"There will be wide-ranging celebrations and the Inonu stadium will definitely be overflowing this evening," said a spokeswoman for Istanbul's Islamist mayor, who is overseeing the week-long celebrations.

The "Conquest Week" reaches its climax on Thursday with an evening of concerts and speeches -- speakers include Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan -- in central Istanbul's Inonu stadium, capped by a recreation of the conquest of Istanbul.
Sultan Mehmet the Conqueror marched into then Byzantine Constantinople 544 years ago on May 29 to lay claim to the city for the Ottoman empire following a 54-day seige.

The celebrations kicked off on Sunday, when a large crowd of people dressed as Ottomans dragged two wooden ships, mounted on wheels, across central Istanbul to the waters of the Golden Horn, as Mehmet's troops are said to have done after the Byzantines blocked off the sea entrance from the Bosphorus.
On Thursday, Istanbul's Islamist mayor, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and his entourage will tour the city, visiting Mehmet's tomb and planting a flag on the ancient city walls.

The conquest celebrations have grown since Erdogan won his seat in 1994, and have grown since his Islam-based Welfare Party came a narrow first in polls in December 1995 and finally struck a coalition deal with the conservatives in June last year.

Political observers say this year's festivities, which coincide with speculation that Erbakan's government will finally collapse under pressure from the powerful secularist military and the establishment, are likely to become his showcase.
"Let's meet at Inonu," said the pro-Welfare Milli Gazete on its front page. "Conquest is the symbol of moving onward and upward ... Without Islam, there would not have been a conquest."

"Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who represents the superiority of the people and not brute force, will be making a speech," Milli Gazete said, pointing out that this would be Erbakan's first "conquest" as prime minister.

Erbakan has in the past raised secularist hackles by claiming that the Islamists would "re-conquer" Istanbul with the building of a mosque in central Taksim square, seen as the symbol of a modern, European Turkey.

Secularist newspapers largely ignored the celebrations, confining the subject to reports of how Istanbul traffic would be disrupted by Erdogan's cortege, shocked accounts of a concert combining classical western music and an Ottoman "Mehter" military band and articles on how Mehmet -- who is admired by Islamists -- liked "un-Islamic" wine and was probably bisexual.
One columnist, Necati Dogru, bemoaned the lack of interest of secularists that has delivered the glory of the conquest into the hands of the Islamists.

"Istanbul ... has always been a world city. Seventy-two languages are spoken here. It seems rather strange to abandon the celebrations of the conquest of this magical city to the excitement and revelry of just one point of view," Dogru wrote in Sabah newspaper.

As part of the festivities, the mayor of Eminonu district is due to distribute gold coins at Sultanahmet square under the shadow of the huge Hagia Sofia church, which Mehmet converted into a mosque on entering the city and where he proclaimed after a prayer: "Hereafter my capital is Istanbul."
Earlier this week, Erdogan spoke of the peace and brotherhood which reigned in the wake of the conquest and asked that politicians of the day take note of this example.

He will not be referring to the immediate aftermath, though, which according to writers then saw blood run down the gutters towards the Golden Horn, staining the waters, and severed heads bobbing up and down near the shoreline like rotten melons.
